title: Webb Just Revealed a Terrifying Cosmic Cat's Head
syntax: {spoken|shown} lets the TTS read one form while subtitles display another.

segments.text: {Seven and a half thousand|7,500} light-years away, something is staring back at us.
It has a head. Two pointed ears. And a single glowing eye.
And the James Webb Space Telescope has just shown us what it really is.

On October {twenty-ninth|29th}, {twenty twenty-six|2026}, NASA and {E S A|ESA} released a new image from two of the greatest telescopes ever built. Hubble and Webb, looking at the very same patch of sky.
Astronomers nicknamed it the Cat's Head Nebula. And once you see the cat, you can't unsee it.
A dark, narrow pillar of dust. A head turned aside. A tail trailing down. And that eye.
But this is no monster. It's something far stranger: a snapshot of stars being born, and of the forces tearing their birthplace apart.
First, where is it? The cat lives inside the Carina Nebula, about {seven and a half thousand|7,500} light-years away, in the southern constellation Carina, the Keel.
The nebula is roughly {three hundred|300} light-years across, and home to at least a dozen stars {fifty to a hundred|50 to 100} times the mass of our Sun.
Here's the key idea. Stars form inside cold clouds of gas and dust. Gravity pulls clumps together, until a new star switches on.
But the hottest, most massive stars don't just shine. They blast out intense ultraviolet radiation and powerful winds.
That radiation heats nearby gas until it literally evaporates. Astronomers call it photoevaporation.
Thin gas vanishes quickly. Denser clumps resist longer. What's left are pillars, sculpted by light.
To see this scene properly, we need two kinds of vision. In visible light, dust is the problem. Tiny grains scatter and absorb it, so thick dust looks like a black wall.
Webb is built for infrared. Longer wavelengths slip past many of those grains, so Webb can see where Hubble can't.
Near-infrared looks through the thinner dust. Mid-infrared sees the dust itself, glowing with warmth.
Three views. Three ways of seeing the same cat.
Start with Hubble. In visible light, the cat is almost completely opaque: a dark brown pillar of dust, blocking everything behind it.

Along its right edge runs a faint, hazy yellow rim. That's gas lit up and ionised by ultraviolet light from nearby massive stars. It's consistent with photoevaporation in action. The cat's skin is being stripped away.
And the glowing red eye? Astronomers think it may be a young star, still partly buried in dust.

Hubble's filters pick out light from oxygen, hydrogen and sulfur. That's why the background shifts from blue and cyan at the top, to yellow, orange and red toward the bottom. It's a map of hot, excited gas.
Now switch to Webb's near-infrared camera. Watch what happens to the dust.
The pillar becomes more transparent. Its complex surface structure appears. And around it, a dense scattering of stars, shown in blue and yellow.
Even a few faint background galaxies show up, seen partly through our own Milky Way.
And the eye? Still there. Still conspicuous, even in infrared.
Then comes mid-infrared, from Webb's {Miri|MIRI} instrument. Now we're not looking through the dust. We're looking at the dust.
Warm grains and carbon-based molecules glow, outlining delicate globules and strands on the cat's left side. Fragile structures, exposed to radiation from nearby massive stars.

The filament turns bluish gray. The background glows red. And the eye turns white. Those colours are assigned, by the way: {Miri|MIRI}'s filters at {seven point seven|7.7}, {eleven|11} and {fifteen|15} micrometres are mapped to blue, green and red.
So let's zoom in on that eye.
If it is a young star, it's an infant. Stars like this form when a dense knot of gas collapses under its own gravity, wrapped in a cocoon of dust that hides the newborn from visible light.
In Webb's mid-infrared image, just to the right of the pillar, there's another bright source. Yellow, against a reddish glow. It's likely an infant star too, embedded in dust.
A narrow filament seems to cross right over it. Are the two connected? Honestly, the image alone can't tell us. That's exactly the kind of question astronomers will chase next.

There's another puzzle near the cat's belly. In Webb's near-infrared image, there's a faint, jet-like feature. It could be gas blasted out by a young star. Or it could be something else. Its origin is uncertain.
And that uncertainty is what makes this image so valuable. It isn't just beautiful. It's a catalogue of open questions.

One quick warning: this is not the Cat's Paw Nebula, which Webb imaged last year. That one sits in Scorpius, roughly {four thousand|4,000} light-years away. The Cat's Head is in Carina, nearly twice as far.

And how big is this scene? Hubble's view is about {two point four|2.4} arcminutes across, which works out to around {five and a half|5.5} light-years. Light itself would need five and a half years to cross it.
And the light we're seeing left this place about {seven and a half thousand|7,500} years ago. Before the first cities. Before writing. It has been travelling toward us all that time.
Now for the part that makes this cat truly haunting.
It isn't permanent.
NASA and {E S A|ESA} are clear about this. The Cat's Head is a temporary scene. The same ultraviolet light and stellar winds that sculpted its shape are still eating away at it.
The denser material inside the pillar resists erosion, at least for now.
Think about what that means. The massive stars nearby are both sculptor and destroyer. Their radiation helped carve the cat, and it will help dismantle it.
And yet, inside it, a young star may be quietly switching on. The very cloud that's being destroyed may be the nursery of something new.
Creation and destruction, side by side, in a shape we happen to read as a face.
No creature. No monster. Just physics, light, and time. And for one brief astronomical moment, a cat.
So the next time someone shows you a face in the stars, remember: it's a star-forming cloud, being pulled apart by light.
Subscribe to Technical Talk India, and tell me in the comments: what do you see in this nebula?
